title: Data from: Paradoxical effects of opioids in suppression of colonic motility
abstract: Opiates reduce colonic motility and transit, but mechanisms for these actions are not understood fully, and opiate-induced constipation is difficult to manage.  Opiate receptors, m (MOR), d (DOR) and k (KOR), are expressed by enteric neurons, and suppression of excitatory cholinergic motor neurons is thought to explain why these drugs reduce colonic transit.  We found that receptor-specific opioid agonists (MOR, DOR and KOR) increase contractions of colonic muscles from mouse proximal and distal colon, effects not easily explained by suppression of excitatory neural input.  Enhancement of contractions was inhibited by tetrodotoxin, L-NNA or apamin (distal colon).  The MOR agonist, EM-1, suppressed spontaneous activity of nitric oxide synthase (NOS+) neurons during the period of tonic inhibition. Neurogenic contractions were also suppressed by EM-1.  MOR were expressed abundantly by NOS+ neurons.  MOR were also expressed in neurons with choline acetyltransferase (ChAT), but the functions of ChAT+ myenteric neurons is diverse and undelineated by our experiments.  EM-1 enhanced Ca2+~~ transients in ICC, caused significant depolarization of membrane potentials of circular muscle cells and reduced post-stimulus depolarization resulting upon cessation of enteric inhibitory nerve stimulation.  These observations demonstrate that the major effects of MOR agonists are suppression of enteric inhibitory neurons and tonic inhibition.  Suppression of excitatory cholinergic motor neurons by EM-1 was not observed. All opioid agonists tested reduced or suppressed colonic migrating motor complexes (CMMCs).  Our results suggest that inhibition of propulsive contractions in the colon by opioids occurs through suppression enteric inhibitory neurons and reduction in tonic inhibition.
